title: Everything perishes but His face
hookLine: all on earth passes, and the face of your Lord remains, full of majesty and honor (55:26–27)

lines: THE CAFÉ CLOSED. THE DOG IS GONE.
cards: Open the photos on your phone and scroll back ten years. The café in that picture closed. The dog is gone.
The friend in the corner moved across the world. Even the phone that took it is in a drawer somewhere, dead. Nothing stayed as it was, not even the light.
In the middle of all its gifts, Surah Ar-Rahman says this out loud, in two short verses. Then it names the one thing it says does not pass.

teach.b: Verses twenty-six and twenty-seven. Pickthall: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory."
In Arabic: kullu man 'alayha fan, wa yabqa wajhu rabbika dhul-jalali wal-ikram. Fan means passing away; yabqa, remains. Two verbs, set against each other.
And the one who remains is described with a phrase that comes back in daily prayer: dhul-jalali wal-ikram, Possessor of Majesty and Honor.

A hadith in Muslim records that on finishing the prayer, the Prophet ﷺ would say a short line ending: blessed are You, Possessor of Majesty and Honor. So this verse's phrase lives in the routine of prayer.

teach.h: WHAT FACE MEANS: MORE THAN ONE READING.
teach.b: What does face mean here? Muslims have answered in more than one way. Some Sunni theologians affirm the face as an attribute of God, real but unlike anything created, without asking how.
Others read face as God's very self, his essence. And some commentators add a third layer: what remains is whatever was done for God's face, for his sake.
Surah Al-Qasas uses the same word: everything perishes except his face. Now notice where the verses sit. Right after them comes the refrain: which of your Lord's favors will you deny?

teach.h: PASSING AWAY, LISTED AS A FAVOR.
teach.b: Passing away is listed among the favors. Commentators explain it in different ways, but one reading is this: if everything here lasted forever, nothing would point beyond itself.
Because things pass, they make room to notice what stays.

how: Many Muslims say a short remembrance after the obligatory prayer that ends with 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor', following the hadith in Sahih Muslim.

o: the face of God, which remains when all passes
a veil worn to cover the face in prayer
the direction Muslims turn to face in prayer

games.q: what passes and what remains — tap the pairs.

s: the phrase 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor' is said after the prayer, following a hadith
a hadith in Muslim records the Prophet saying it after the prayer.
all Muslim scholars read 'face' the same way
some affirm it as an attribute without asking how, some read it as God's self, some add 'what is done for his sake'.
the refrain is never placed after these verses about passing
it comes right after them: passing away is listed among the favors.

games.q: the surah has just said that everything on earth passes. what follows?
o: the refrain: which of your Lord's favors will you deny?
a list of what will last on earth.
games.why: passing away is listed among the favors, and the refrain follows. commentators explain why in different ways.

practice: Pick up something near you, a cup of tea going cold, a pen running low, or just your own open hand, and hold it lightly, knowing it won't last, without gripping harder.
If you pray, you can say quietly, ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram, O Possessor of Majesty and Honor, the words from the hadith; if not, simply hold it and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Wajh: the face of God, full of majesty and honor, which 55:27 says remains after everything on earth has passed away. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and the face of your Lord remains. yabqa, remains, set against fan, passing away.

carryVoice: Your line: his face remains. Passing away, too, is listed among the favors. That's day six hundred seven.
